title: A candidate that retries in the same term, proved safe, and shown never to elect a leader
summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one in a new term. A developer makes it ask again in the same term instead, for the votes it lacks, so that a candidate that cannot win does not drive the whole cluster's term up on every timeout. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change safe under three of its configurations: one leader per term, with three servers, by induction, and with four. The fourth configuration, the liveness check, finds the run the safety proofs cannot see: three servers whose timers fire together are three candidates of term 1, each refused by the other two, and under this rule nothing ever starts term 2. The cluster has no leader, for good. A green safety result says exactly what it checked; the liveness property says the rest.

change.description: Split the `ElectionTimeout` case by role: a follower runs as before; a candidate retries with `REQUEST_VOTES` alone, keeping its term, its vote and its tally. The reasoning in the comment: every retry in a new term forces every server to adopt that term, and a candidate that cannot reach a majority, partitioned or slow, inflates the cluster's term on every timeout (the disruptive server of Ongaro's thesis, section 4.2.3). The behavioural contract is regenerated and its diff is the one case `decide(CANDIDATE, ElectionTimeout[])`, whose effects lose `INCREMENT_TERM` and `VOTE_FOR_SELF`; a test for the new effects is added. The reviewer approves the diff.

risk: Safety is intact, and the model proves it: the candidate keeps its term, its vote and a tally whose votes were all cast in that term, so nothing it counts is stale and nothing it does lets anyone vote twice. What is lost is the one thing a new term is for. Raft resolves a split vote, two or more candidates of one term that each hold their own vote and cannot reach a majority, by having each start a new election in a new term after a randomized timeout, so that one of them is first to ask a cluster whose votes are free again (section 5.2). Under this rule the candidates of a split term ask the same servers for the same votes, already cast, forever; nothing increments the term until a follower's timer fires, and in a cluster where every server is a candidate there is no follower. Three servers that time out together are a cluster with no leader, for good. That is a liveness failure: no state is wrong, no step is wrong, and the run never ends. An invariant cannot say it, an action property cannot say it, and the inductive invariant cannot say it; only a property of whole runs can, and the model has two, checked under fairness conditions that say what each server is assumed to get round to.
explanation: The election model's role machine is generated from the behavioural contract of the patched `RoleMachine#decide`, which the tool proves the bytecode satisfies on all 52 inputs. Under three servers and three terms every invariant and both action properties hold, and there are fewer reachable states than with the committed rule, since a candidate no longer leaves its term on its own; the inductive step holds, since a candidate's retry changes nothing the invariant mentions; four servers under the symmetry set hold too. The liveness configuration checks the same three-server model under the fairness conditions `Fairness` (a server whose timer nothing resets times out, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, a leader sends its heartbeats) and finds a run that breaks `ALeaderIsElected`, the property that a run which stays within the term budget elects a leader: s3's timer fires, then s1's, then s2's, each starting term 1 with a vote for itself, and the run stays in that state forever (TLC's `Stuttering`). Every term is 1, well within the budget; no leader ever comes. Fairness demands nothing more of it: each candidate's retry is a step that changes nothing, so no timer is enabled in the sense that matters, and each canvass is refused, since every vote of term 1 is cast. With the committed rule the same three timers firing together start term 2 on the next timeout, and the first candidate to ask a server whose vote is free again wins. TLC names the property after rerunning each temporal property alone.
resolution: Revert. The rule the developer wanted is pre-vote (thesis, sections 4.2.3 and 9.6): a candidate first asks whether it could win, without incrementing its term, and starts the election only if a majority says yes, which spares the cluster the term inflation without touching the retry. The liveness property is the one to keep in mind for any retry rule: a retry that does not start a new term cannot end a split vote, because the votes of the split term are cast. What the property does not say is also worth reading: it is conditioned on the term budget, because a model without a clock cannot show that a leader comes within any number of terms (every term can split, and Raft's answer is randomized timeouts), and it holds under the fairness conditions stated with it and no others. The example sits next to 062, where the three safety configurations find a bug, and 064, where all four configurations hold.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.

`RaftElectionLive.cfg` checks liveness under fairness: a timer nothing resets fires, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, a leader sends its heartbeats. Each action's enabling condition is written out as a state predicate, so that TLC need not compute `ENABLED` on every step of the liveness check. A retry rule can keep every safety property and still break liveness.
Proved safe under every safety configuration, yet three candidates ask each other forever: a liveness failure only the fairness configuration can state. Compare 064.
provenance: Constructed from the rules for candidates in figure 2 of the Raft paper, by keeping the term on a candidate's retry.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (2014): figure 2, the rules for candidates, and section 5.2, leader election and split votes
Ongaro, Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (2014): chapter 3, the basic algorithm, and section 4.2.3, disruptive servers
Lamport, Specifying Systems, chapter 8: liveness and fairness, and section 14.3.5, checking liveness with TLC
Lamport, Using TLC to Check Inductive Invariance (2018): the invariant as TLC's initial predicate
